kurals.tamil:
உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ் செய்தலால்
கள்ளினும் காமம் இனிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Ullinum theeraap perumakizh seydhalaal
kallinum kaamam inidhu.
kurals.meaning: Love is sweeter than toddy: wine cheers only while it is drunk, but love gives an unfailing great joy even when it is merely remembered.
kurals.elementary: A sweet drink makes you happy only while you are sipping it. But think of a wonderful day with someone you love, and you smile all over again. That is why the poet says love is sweeter than any drink: even the memory of it makes you glad.
kurals.university: Chapter 121, ninaintavar pulampal (‘the lament of those who remember’), stands in the karpiyal (wedded love) sequence on separation, where the absent partner is sustained and tormented by memory. The opening couplet sets the chapter’s premise by comparison with kaḷ (toddy, palm wine): uḷḷiṉum, ‘even when merely thought of’, love yields tīrā perumakiḻ, a great joy that does not run out, whereas kaḷ delights only when consumed, as Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both gloss. Solomon Pappaiah, following the traditional assignment, hears the husband speaking of past union with his wife, while modern readers often extend it to both lovers. Pope renders: ‘From thought of her unfailing gladness springs, / Sweeter than palm-rice wine the joy love brings.’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the second canto of Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Radha, left alone in a bower after Krishna has wandered off with other cowherd girls, dwells in song on her memories of him, and her heart takes delight in recalling his play even as she grieves.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s Radha shows how, in the bhakti love lyric, remembering the beloved is itself a source of rapture.
hinduism.tie_back: Radha’s memory-song illustrates the Kural’s claim that love delights even when it is only thought of.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Canto 2 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Barbara Stoler Miller)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known canto; strong fit on the sweetness of remembered love, though Radha’s memory is mixed with jealousy and lacks the Kural’s comparison with wine.

christianity.quote_or_event: “We will remember thy love more than wine: the upright love thee.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song of Solomon says that she and her companions will remember the beloved’s love more than wine.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts set the remembrance of love above the pleasure of wine, the Kural’s exact comparison.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; near one-to-one, combining remembering, love and the comparison with wine.

islam.quote_or_event: The Sufi poet Ibn al-Farid opens his Wine Ode by saying that, in remembrance of the Beloved, he and his companions drank a wine that made them drunk before ever the vine was created.
islam.explanation: In the Khamriyya, the intoxication of love is a wine that comes from remembering the Beloved, needing no cup.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, Ibn al-Farid makes love-remembered a better intoxicant than any drink, though his Beloved is divine.
islam.source: Ibn al-Farid, al-Khamriyya (The Wine Ode), opening verse (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry and R.A. Nicholson)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous opening line; strong imagistic fit, though the Sufi poem is mystical rather than conjugal.

judaism.quote_or_event: “How fair is thy love, my sister, my bride! How much better is thy love than wine!”
judaism.explanation: The lover of the Song of Songs ranks his bride’s love above wine.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s verdict that love is sweeter than toddy is the same judgment, made in a Tamil key.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); close match on love over wine, though without the Kural’s point that memory alone suffices.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada traces grief and fear to endearment and praises freedom from it.
buddhism.tie_back: Where the Kural calls remembered love an unfailing joy, the Buddha warns that such endearment is the very root of sorrow, a deliberate contrast.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a contrasting rather than parallel teaching, offered as the most relevant Buddhist view.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the dialogue of the priest’s sons, the youths tell their father that pleasures bring a moment’s happiness but long and intense suffering, and so are a hindrance to liberation.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana treats every sensual joy, love included, as brief sweetness bought with long pain.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural praises love for a joy that never runs out; Jain teaching answers that such joy is fleeting and binding, a candid contrast.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.13 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of a well-known verse, not checked live; a contrasting Jain view rather than a parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho says that some call an army of horsemen or of ships the loveliest thing on the dark earth, but she says it is whatever one loves, and she recalls the absent Anactoria, whose lovely walk and shining face she would rather see than all the chariots of Lydia.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho ranks the beloved above every rival splendour, and does so by remembering someone far away.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s speaker, Sappho finds love, recalled in absence, sweeter than anything else the world offers.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho, fragment 16 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Anne Carson)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested fragment; strong fit on love remembered as the supreme delight.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that lovers take pleasure in talking, writing and composing about the absent beloved, because in remembering him they seem to perceive him, and that love begins when one delights not only in the beloved’s presence but in remembering him when absent.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, remembered love is a genuine pleasure and even the mark that love has begun.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point in analytic form: love gives joy even when it is only thought of.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric 1.11, 1370b (paraphrase; cf. tr. W. Rhys Roberts)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a specific passage; near one-to-one on the pleasure of remembering an absent beloved.

kurals.tamil:
எனைத்தொன்று இனிதேகாண் காமம்தாம் வீழ்வார்
நினைப்ப வருவதொன்று இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Enaiththondru inidhekaan kaamamdhaam veezhvaar
ninaippa varuvadhondru il.
kurals.meaning: See how sweet love is in every way: when one thinks of the person one loves, no pain of separation comes at all.
kurals.elementary: When your best friend moves away, you miss them. But when you think about the funny games you played together, the sad feeling goes away for a while. The poet says love is like that: just thinking of the person you love can chase the sadness off.
kurals.university: The couplet explains why love is sweet ‘in every way’ (eṉaittoṉṟu): to think of those one desires (tām vīḻvār) brings no suffering (varuvatu oṉṟu il), so love delights both in union and in separation; Parimelazhagar, who treats it as a continuation of the previous couplet’s speaker, says Valluvar called it sweet ‘in any measure’ because it is equally sweet when lovers are together and apart. Manakkudavar and Parip Perumal instead make it the heroine’s rejoinder to a confidante who warns that her pining will harm her. There is a genuine textual variant: Perundevanar, commenting on the Virasoliyam, quotes the second line as niṉaikka varuvatu oṉṟu uṇṭu (‘there is something that comes when one thinks’), whereas Parimelazhagar reads niṉaippa varuvatu oṉṟu il, the standard text (as given on kuralthiran.com). Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the head-word with typographical slips (eṉaittoṉaṟu, and ēl for il), which are corrected here against kuralthiran.com and the commentaries’ glosses.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gopi Gita the cowherd women, searching for the vanished Krishna, tell him that the nectar of his words and of stories about him gives life to those burning with separation and removes their sins.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis find that dwelling on Krishna, through his words and his stories, revives them even while he is absent.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s claim that thinking of the beloved banishes separation’s pain is exactly the gopis’ comfort.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous verse; strong fit on remembrance soothing the pain of separation, in a devotional frame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips: When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist, far from the sanctuary, finds his soul satisfied simply by remembering God through the night.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, remembrance of the one loved turns absence into satisfaction instead of pain.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; good fit on comforting remembrance, though the object is God rather than a spouse.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those who have believed and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allāh. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allāh hearts are assured.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that hearts find rest and assurance in remembering God (dhikr).
islam.tie_back: The Kural finds that remembering the beloved leaves no room for pain; the Qur’an finds the same calming power in remembering God.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via quran.com API; a parallel on the soothing power of remembrance, but the remembered one is God, not a human lover.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.”
judaism.explanation: Jacob’s love for Rachel made seven years of labour and waiting feel like a few days.
judaism.tie_back: Jacob shows the Kural’s truth that love takes the sting out of waiting and separation.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); good thematic fit on love easing a long separation, though it does not speak of remembering.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells his monks that if fear or terror arises when they are alone in the forest, they should recollect him, the Teacher, and their fear will vanish, just as Sakka’s warriors lose fear by looking at their king’s banner.
buddhism.explanation: Recollection of the Buddha (buddhanussati) is taught as a remedy that dispels fear and distress when one is alone.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, calling to mind one who is dear removes the pain of being alone, though the Buddhist object is the Teacher, not a lover.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutta; parallel mechanism of comforting recollection in solitude, different object.

jainism.quote_or_event: Manatunga tells the Jina that, let alone hymns of praise, even the telling of his story destroys the sins of living beings, as the sun’s light, though far away, opens lotuses in the pond.
jainism.explanation: The Bhaktamara Stotra teaches that merely calling the Jina to mind, through his story, has a cleansing, healing effect.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s comfort in thinking of the beloved has a Jain devotional echo in the healing power of remembering the Jina, though the Jina neither returns nor responds.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of a widely recited hymn, not checked live; only a structural parallel, since Jain devotion is not romantic.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho recalls a girl who wept as she left her, and answers her farewell by telling her to go happily and remember, reminding her of the garlands, perfumes and soft beds they once shared.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho uses shared memories as the consolation for parting.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural, too, offers memory of the loved one as the cure for separation’s pain.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho, fragment 94 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Anne Carson)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested fragment; strong fit on memory as consolation in separation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Dying in great pain, Epicurus writes to Idomeneus that against all his suffering he set the gladness of mind that came from remembering their past conversations.
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus held that recollected joys can outweigh present pain.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker uses the same remedy: the memory of the beloved leaves no room for the pain of separation.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 10.22 (letter of Epicurus to Idomeneus) (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous letter; strong fit on remembered joy overcoming pain, though about friendship rather than love.

kurals.tamil:
நினைப்பவர் போன்று நினையார்கொல் தும்மல்
சினைப்பது போன்று கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ninaippavar poandru ninaiyaarkol thummal
sinaippadhu poandru kedum.
kurals.meaning: A sneeze seemed about to come and then died away; is he, who seemed about to think of me, now not thinking of me after all?
kurals.elementary: Some people say that if you sneeze, someone far away is thinking of you. The lady in this poem feels a sneeze coming, and then it goes away! She worries: did he start to think of me and then stop? It is a gentle, funny way to show how much she wants to be remembered.
kurals.university: The image rests on the folk belief, presupposed by all the glosses, that a sneeze signals that someone far away is thinking of one. The heroine feels a sneeze ‘budding’ (ciṉaippatu, from ciṉai, to sprout) and then subsiding (keṭum), and asks whether her husband, seeming to think of her, has stopped (niṉaippavar pōṉṟu niṉaiyār-kol). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all render it this way, and Pope gives: ‘A fit of sneezing threatened, but it passed away; / He seemed to think of me, but do his fancies stray?’ The couplet’s comedy is tender: a trivial bodily flicker becomes evidence in a lover’s anxious inquiry. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Captive in Ravana’s grove and on the point of despair, Sita feels her left eye, left arm and left thigh throb, auspicious signs for a woman, and takes heart that news of Rama is near; Hanuman soon appears.
hinduism.explanation: The Ramayana treats involuntary bodily twitches as omens about an absent husband.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita reads a throb as the Kural’s heroine reads a sneeze: as a sign of whether her distant husband is near in thought.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, sarga 29 (paraphrase; cf. valmikiramayan.net)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; strong fit on reading a bodily omen about the absent beloved, though Sita’s omen is fulfilled while the heroine’s fades.

christianity.quote_or_event: “O Ephraim, what shall I do unto thee? O Judah, what shall I do unto thee? for your goodness is as a morning cloud, and as the early dew it goeth away.”
christianity.explanation: God laments that his people’s devotion appears and then vanishes like morning dew.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine fears the same thing: an affection that seemed about to arrive, then went away like the half-sneeze.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; matches the image of love that starts and fades, but with no omen and in a covenantal setting.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that when someone sneezes he should say ‘Praise be to God’, and the one who hears should answer ‘May God have mercy on you’, to which the sneezer replies with a prayer for guidance.
islam.explanation: Islam turns the sneeze into an occasion for praise and mutual blessing rather than an omen.
islam.tie_back: The Kural reads a sneeze as a sign of a lover’s thought; Islamic etiquette, by contrast, answers every sneeze with remembrance of God.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith; matches only on the sneeze itself, offered as the nearest Islamic treatment.

judaism.quote_or_event: A rabbinic tradition holds that before Jacob a person never fell ill: he would sneeze and his soul would leave him, until Jacob prayed for illness as a warning before death; hence the custom of answering a sneeze with a blessing for life.
judaism.explanation: Jewish lore treats the sneeze as a portentous moment bound up with life itself.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, this tradition invests a sneeze with hidden meaning, though about life and death rather than love.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a midrashic tradition from memory; the shared element is the sneeze as omen, not love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the Buddha sneezed while teaching and the monks loudly called out ‘Long life to you, Lord!’, he asked whether saying so could make anyone live or die, and told them not to say it; later he allowed it in answer to laypeople’s courtesy.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha gently debunks the belief that words spoken at a sneeze have real power.
buddhism.tie_back: Against the Kural’s playful omen-reading, the Buddha questions whether a sneeze means anything at all.
buddhism.source: Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga V.33 (paraphrase; cf. tr. T.W. Rhys Davids and H. Oldenberg, SBE 20)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a Vinaya episode from memory; a direct engagement with sneeze-belief, but sceptical rather than parallel.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Kalpa Sutra tells how Queen Trishala saw fourteen great dreams, among them an elephant, a bull, a lion and the full moon, which interpreters explained as signs that she would bear a son destined to be a great king or a Jina.
jainism.explanation: Jain narrative treats signs given to the body and mind as genuine portents of what is coming.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine reads her half-sneeze as a sign; Trishala’s dreams are the classic Jain case of reading omens, though about a birth, not a lover.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira, the fourteen dreams (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; only a loose parallel on omens, with no romantic content.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Penelope wishes aloud that Odysseus would come home, Telemachus sneezes loudly so that the house rings; she laughs and takes it as a sign that the suitors will meet their doom, not knowing that Odysseus is already in the hall in disguise.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer a sneeze at the right moment is an omen about the absent husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope and the Kural’s heroine both read a sneeze as news of a husband far away in body but near in fate or thought.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 17.541-547 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a specific passage; strong parallel on sneeze-omen tied to an absent husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that anything whatever may accidentally become a cause of hope or fear, and that this is why people interpret chance things as omens.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza explains omen-reading as the mind attaching hope and fear to whatever happens to accompany them.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s anxious reading of a sneeze is a perfect instance of hope and fear fastening on a chance sign.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part III, Proposition 50 and Scholium (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a specific proposition; it explains the Kural’s psychology rather than sharing its feeling.

kurals.tamil:
யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து எந்நெஞ்சத்து
ஓஒ உளரே அவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Yaamum ulaengol avarnenjaththu ennenjaththu
oo-o ulare avar.
kurals.meaning: He lives always in my heart, alas; do I too have a place in his?
kurals.elementary: Imagine you think about your grandma every single day while she is far away. You might wonder, ‘Does Grandma think about me too?’ The lady in this poem asks the same: he is always in my heart, but am I in his?
kurals.university: The couplet sets two hearts side by side: avar neñcattu (‘in his heart’) and en neñcattu (‘in my heart’). The exclamation ōo (lengthened ō, ‘alas’ or ‘oh!’) marks her certainty that he is unceasingly present in her own heart (uḷarē avar), while the particle kol turns her own presence in his heart into an anxious question (yāmum uḷēṅ-kol). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘do we too remain without leaving in his heart?’, and Pope renders: ‘Have I a place within his heart? / From mine, alas! he never doth depart.’ The royal plural yām is the heroine’s usual self-reference in the Kamattuppal. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s play, Shakuntala composes a love letter to King Dushyanta, saying that she does not know his heart, but that love torments her day and night because her heart is set on him.
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala is certain of her own love but uncertain of his, and writes to find out.
hinduism.tie_back: Her ‘I know not your heart, but mine is yours’ is the Kural’s question in dramatic form.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Abhijnanashakuntalam, Act 3 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; strong fit on the asymmetry between known and unknown hearts.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even as it is meet for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, writing from prison, tells his distant friends that he holds them in his heart.
christianity.tie_back: Paul states the half the Kural’s speaker is sure of, that the absent ones dwell in her heart, without her doubt about the other half.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; partial fit on holding the absent in one’s heart, without the romantic uncertainty.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi teaches that no lover seeks union without the beloved also seeking him: when the lightning of love has struck this heart, know that there is love in that heart too.
islam.explanation: The Masnavi assures the lover that longing in one heart implies longing in the other.
islam.tie_back: Rumi answers the Kural’s anxious question with confidence: if he is in your heart, you are in his.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book III (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known teaching; exact verse numbers not checked live, so the citation is to the book only.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Set me as a seal upon thy heart, As a seal upon thine arm; For love is strong as death.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved asks to be set as a seal on her lover’s heart, permanently impressed there.
judaism.tie_back: This is the wish behind the Kural’s question: to be held in the beloved’s heart as he is held in hers.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); strong fit on wishing a place in the beloved’s heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the Buddha returns to Kapilavastu years after leaving home, Yasodhara does not go out to greet him but sends their son Rahula to ask for his inheritance, saying ‘That is your father.’
buddhism.explanation: The wife left behind by the future Buddha waits to see whether he still holds a place for her and their son.
buddhism.tie_back: Yasodhara, who kept her husband in her heart through his long absence, embodies the Kural’s question whether she remains in his.
buddhism.source: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga I.54 (paraphrase; cf. tr. T.W. Rhys Davids and H. Oldenberg, SBE 13)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical episode; the inner question is implied by later tradition rather than stated in the Vinaya.

jainism.quote_or_event: The poet of the Kalyanamandira Stotra tells the Jina that when he dwells in a devotee’s heart, even tight bonds of karma loosen at once, as snakes coiled round a sandalwood tree slip away when a peacock arrives.
jainism.explanation: Jain devotional poetry speaks of the Jina abiding in the heart of the devotee and transforming it.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine is sure her beloved dwells in her heart; the Jain devotee speaks of the Jina dwelling in his, though without any hope of a place in the Jina’s.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not checked live; matches only on the beloved dwelling in the heart, since the Jina, free of attachment, keeps no one in his.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s letter, Laodamia writes to her husband Protesilaus at Troy, telling him he is always before her mind, and anxiously wondering what he is doing and whether he remembers her among the fighting.
greek_mythology.explanation: Laodamia’s letter is full of the asymmetry between her constant thought and her uncertainty about his.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Her question is the Kural’s: you never leave my mind, but do I stay in yours?
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s general content; strong fit on the anxious wife abroad in thought, line numbers not given.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Montaigne, writing of his friend La Boétie, says their souls were so mingled and blended that the seam joining them could no longer be found, and that if pressed to say why he loved him, he could only answer: because it was he, because it was I.
philosophy.explanation: Montaigne describes a love so mutual that each soul dwells wholly in the other.
philosophy.tie_back: Montaigne’s fulfilled mutuality is what the Kural’s heroine hopes for when she asks whether she lives in his heart as he lives in hers.
philosophy.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays 1.28, ‘Of Friendship’ (paraphrase; cf. tr. Charles Cotton)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous essay; it supplies the answer the heroine longs for, about friendship rather than marriage.

kurals.tamil:
தம்நெஞ்சத்து எம்மைக் கடிகொண்டார் நாணார்கொல்
எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thamnenjaththu emmaik katikondaar naanaarkol
emnenjaththu ovaa varal.
kurals.meaning: He has barred me from his own heart; is he not ashamed to keep coming into mine without a pause?
kurals.elementary: Imagine a friend who never lets you into their clubhouse, but keeps walking into yours whenever they like! The lady in this poem jokes that her husband does that with hearts: he keeps visiting her thoughts all day, but she wonders if he lets her into his.
kurals.university: The couplet turns the previous question into a playful accusation. Kaṭi koṇṭār means ‘those who have set a guard against’ (kaṭi, ‘watch, prohibition’): Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘he who has kept guard in his heart so that we may not enter’, and Pope renders ‘Me from his heart he jealously excludes: / Hath he no shame who ceaseless on my heart intrudes?’ Ōvā varal is ‘coming without ceasing’, and nāṇār-kol asks ‘is he not ashamed?’, invoking nāṇ, the sense of shame and propriety prized in the Kural. The reproach is affectionate: his constant ‘visits’ are simply her inability to stop thinking of him. One modern gloss (Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh.com) reads kaṭi as ‘scold’, but the guarding sense is standard. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhramara Gita, a gopi addresses a bee she takes for Krishna’s messenger, scolding Krishna for forgetting the women of Vraja after leaving them, while confessing that they cannot give up talking and thinking of him.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis rebuke Krishna for his indifference even as they admit he fills their minds.
hinduism.tie_back: The gopi’s complaint is the Kural’s: he shuts us out of his heart, yet will not leave ours.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.47.12-21, Bhramara Gita (paraphrase; cf. vedabase.io)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; strong fit on reproaching the beloved who forgets yet remains constantly in mind.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
christianity.explanation: The bride finds her beloved withdrawn and unresponsive, though her whole soul goes out to him.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved seems closed to her while she remains wholly open and occupied with him.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; good fit on one-sided openness, though without the Kural’s playful reproach.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn Hazm devotes chapters of The Ring of the Dove to the pain of loving one who turns away, describing lovers whose thoughts are never free of a beloved who keeps them at a distance.
islam.explanation: The Andalusian scholar analyses one-sided love and the beloved’s aloofness as recognised stages of love.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, barred from his heart but haunted by him in hers, is a case Ibn Hazm describes.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapters on aversion and separation (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)
islam._accuracy_note: General paraphrase of the treatise’s themes, chapter numbers not checked live; thematically apt but not a specific matching passage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved seeks her lover through the night and cannot find him.
judaism.tie_back: Her lover fills her nights as the Kural’s husband fills his wife’s heart, yet he is nowhere to be reached.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); partial fit on unanswered longing, without the reproach of shamelessness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that when a man who longs for sensual objects is frustrated in his desire, he is afflicted as if pierced by an arrow.
buddhism.explanation: Desire that is not met in return becomes a wound that keeps returning to the mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The beloved who keeps ‘coming’ into her heart is, in Buddhist terms, the dart of unfulfilled longing.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 4.1, Kama Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a short sutta; diagnoses the experience rather than sharing the Kural’s tender reproach.

jainism.quote_or_event: Prince Pavananjaya, offended on the eve of his marriage, neglects his bride Anjana for twenty-two years, never speaking to her, while she remains devoted to him in thought, until he finally realises her grief and returns to her.
jainism.explanation: The Jain Ramayana tradition tells of a wife wholly given in heart to a husband who has shut her out of his.
jainism.tie_back: Anjana lives the Kural’s situation exactly: excluded from his heart, while he never leaves hers.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 7, story of Anjana and Pavananjaya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson); also in Vimalasuri’s Paumacariya
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative, not re-checked live this session; strong fit on one-sided devotion to an aloof husband.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s letter, Phyllis writes to Demophoon, who promised to return to her within a month and has not come, reproaching him for forgetting her while she counts the days and watches the sea for his sails.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phyllis is consumed by thought of a lover who seems to have put her out of his mind.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She makes the Kural’s complaint: he has no room for me, yet I can think of nothing but him.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s general content; good fit, though Phyllis’s tone is bitter where the Kural’s is playful.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius observes that even when the one you love is absent, images of the beloved are still present and the sweet name keeps sounding in your ears.
philosophy.explanation: For Lucretius the beloved’s image keeps returning to the mind unbidden, which is why love is hard to escape.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s husband who ‘comes ceaselessly’ into his wife’s heart is Lucretius’s haunting image of the absent beloved.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things 4.1061-1062 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.E. Leonard)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a specific passage; strong fit on the beloved’s image intruding unbidden, though Lucretius treats it as a malady to be cured.

kurals.tamil:
மற்றியான் என்னுளேன் மன்னோ அவரொடியான்
உற்றநாள் உள்ள உளேன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Matriyaan ennulen manno avarodiyaan
utranaal ulla ulen.
kurals.meaning: I stay alive only by remembering the days I spent with him; by what else could I live?
kurals.elementary: When someone you love is far away, you might look at photos of happy times together to feel better. The lady in this poem says remembering their happy days is what keeps her going, like food that keeps her strong.
kurals.university: The couplet makes memory the very means of survival. Avaroṭu yāṉ uṟṟa nāḷ are ‘the days when I was joined with him’; uḷḷa, ‘by recalling’, I live (uḷēṉ). The first line’s maṟṟu yāṉ eṉṉ uḷēṉ, ‘otherwise, by what do I live?’, carries the particles maṉ and ō, which the commentators treat as expletives adding pathos. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss: ‘It is by thinking of the days I was with him that I am alive; by what else?’ Pope renders: ‘How live I yet? I live to ponder o’er / The days of bliss with him that are no more.’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Held captive in Lanka, Sita endures her grief by fixing her mind on Rama, and when Hanuman finds her, she says she will keep her life only a little longer in the hope of seeing him again.
hinduism.explanation: Sita’s life in captivity is sustained by remembrance of and hope for her husband.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita is the classic Indian image of the Kural’s wife who lives only by thinking of her absent husband.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Sita’s laments and her words to Hanuman) (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: General paraphrase of a famous section, sarga numbers not checked; strong fit on survival through remembrance of the husband.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I thank my God upon every remembrance of you.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells his far-off friends that each time he remembers them he gives thanks.
christianity.tie_back: Remembrance of loved ones sustains Paul in prison as it sustains the Kural’s wife in separation.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; partial fit on sustaining remembrance, without the Kural’s life-or-death intensity.

islam.quote_or_event: Verses attributed to Majnun say that he passes by the dwellings of Layla and kisses this wall and that wall, not because he loves the houses, but for love of the one who once lived in them.
islam.explanation: Majnun keeps his love alive by clinging to every trace of the absent Layla.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife living on memories of days together, Majnun lives on the traces of his beloved’s past presence.
islam.source: Attributed to Qays ibn al-Mulawwah (Majnun Layla), Diwan (paraphrase)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of widely quoted verses whose attribution is traditional rather than certain; good fit on living by traces of the beloved.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I remember the days of old; I meditate on all Thy doing; I muse on the work of Thy hands.”
judaism.explanation: In distress, the psalmist sustains himself by recalling earlier days of God’s nearness.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife, the psalmist survives a time of absence by remembering days of closeness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); parallel use of memory in distress, but addressed to God, not a spouse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: A man whose only son has died goes daily to the cemetery crying ‘Where are you, my only child?’, and the Buddha tells him that sorrow, lamentation and despair are born from those who are dear.
buddhism.explanation: The Piyajatika Sutta shows memory of a lost loved one becoming the man’s whole life, and diagnoses it as the source of grief.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife lives on memories; the Buddha warns that such dependence on the dear is what makes grief.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical sutta; a contrasting diagnosis of the same experience, and about bereavement rather than separation.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain Ramayana, Sita, carried off to Lanka, refuses Ravana and resolves not to take food until she receives news of Rama, holding fast to him in thought.
jainism.explanation: The Jain retelling keeps Sita’s steadfast inner attachment to her husband as the strength that sustains her in captivity.
jainism.tie_back: Sita lives only by her bond with the absent Rama, as the Kural’s wife lives only by memory of their days together.
jainism.source: Vimalasuri, Paumacariya (Jain Ramayana), Sita in Lanka (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of the Jain narrative, chapter not checked live; distinct from the Hindu Valmiki version but close in theme.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope, hearing the bard sing of the Greeks’ return from Troy, asks him to stop, because she always remembers with longing so dear a head, her husband, whose fame is spread throughout Greece.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope’s twenty years of waiting are sustained by constant remembrance of Odysseus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope lives, as the Kural’s wife does, by never ceasing to remember the husband who is away.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 1.337-344 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a specific passage; strong fit on a faithful wife living in memory of her absent husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Laelius, mourning his friend Scipio, says that Scipio still lives for him, that the memory of their friendship and shared life sustains him, and that of all fortune’s gifts nothing compares with that friendship.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero’s Laelius finds in remembered companionship the strength to go on.
philosophy.tie_back: Laelius lives on memories of days with Scipio as the Kural’s wife lives on memories of days with her husband.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the dialogue’s close; strong fit on living by remembered companionship, though about friendship and death.

kurals.tamil:
மறப்பின் எவனாவன் மற்கொல் மறப்பறியேன்
உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Marappin evanaavan markol marappariyaen
ullinum ullam sudum.
kurals.meaning: I have never once forgotten him, and even remembering him scorches my heart; what would become of me if I forgot?
kurals.elementary: Missing someone can hurt a little, like a warm ache inside. But the lady in this poem says that forgetting him would be even worse, because the memories are part of who she is. So she keeps remembering, even though it stings.
kurals.university: The couplet balances two pains. Maṟappu aṟiyēṉ, ‘I know no forgetting’, yet even recalling (uḷḷiṉum) burns the heart (uḷḷam cuṭum), with a characteristic pun on uḷḷu (‘to think’) and uḷḷam (‘heart, mind’); what then would I become if I forgot (maṟappiṉ evaṉ āvaṉ)? Maṟ-kol combines the particles maṉ and kol. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as ‘even remembering without forgetting, the pain of separation burns; if I forgot, how could I live?’, while Puliyur Kesikan (on thirukkural.net) reads ‘if I even think of forgetting, that thought burns’. Pope renders: ‘If I remembered not what were I then? And yet, / The fiery smart of what my spirit knows not to forget!’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Narada Bhakti Sutra gives Narada’s own definition of devotion as offering every act to God and feeling extreme anguish on forgetting him.
hinduism.explanation: In the bhakti tradition, forgetting the beloved Lord is the greatest pain, and unbroken remembrance the mark of love.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine dreads forgetting more than the burn of memory, exactly as Narada makes forgetting the beloved the supreme anguish.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of a well-known sutra, translations vary; strong fit on the anguish of forgetting the beloved, in a devotional frame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Greatly desiring to see thee, being mindful of thy tears, that I may be filled with joy.”
christianity.explanation: Paul remembers Timothy’s tears at their parting, a memory that both pains and draws him with longing.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s memory, like the Kural heroine’s, is painful yet treasured, and it feeds a longing to be reunited.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; partial fit on painful yet cherished memory of parting.

islam.quote_or_event: “They said, ‘By Allāh, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s sons warn him that his unceasing remembrance of the lost Joseph will destroy him, yet he will not stop.
islam.tie_back: Jacob, consumed by a memory he will not give up, is the Kural’s lover who knows no forgetting though remembering burns.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via quran.com API; strong fit on unceasing, consuming remembrance, though of a son rather than a spouse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, Let my right hand forget her cunning. Let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth, If I remember thee not.”
judaism.explanation: The exiles by the rivers of Babylon swear never to forget Jerusalem, though remembering it makes them weep.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, memory is painful, but forgetting would be a kind of self-destruction.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); strong structural fit on refusing to forget though memory grieves, about a city rather than a lover.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Fire Sermon the Buddha teaches that the eye, the mind and all their objects are burning with the fire of passion, aversion and delusion, burning with sorrow, lamentation and despair.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism describes passion and its memories as a literal burning of the mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘memory burns the heart’ is, for the Buddha, the fire of passion that release alone extinguishes.
buddhism.source: Adittapariyaya Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.28 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Nanamoli Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous sutta; shared fire imagery, but the Buddhist remedy is letting go, the very forgetting the heroine fears.

jainism.quote_or_event: Among the conditions for a monk’s chastity, the Uttaradhyayana forbids him to recall the pleasures and amusements he formerly enjoyed with women, since such remembrance inflames desire and endangers his vow.
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic discipline treats the memory of past love as a fire that must not be stirred.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine will not forget though memory burns; Jain teaching tells the renunciant to do the opposite, a candid contrast.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 16 (conditions of brahmacarya) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known lecture, not re-checked live; it sees memory as burning, as the Kural does, but prescribes letting it go.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Hector’s death, Achilles cannot sleep but tosses from side to side, remembering Patroclus, all they had done and suffered together, and weeping as he recalls it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows memory of a beloved companion as an unrelenting torment that Achilles cannot put aside.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ sleepless remembering is the Kural’s burning memory that the lover will not and cannot forget.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 24.3-13 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a specific passage; strong fit on painful, inescapable memory, though of a dead comrade rather than an absent spouse.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates describes how the soul separated from the beautiful beloved is parched and in pain, but when it remembers the beloved’s beauty it rejoices, so that, caught between pain and joy, it is perplexed and cannot rest.
philosophy.explanation: Plato portrays memory of the beloved as at once a torment and a delight.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s double bind: memory burns, yet without it there is nothing to live by.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 251c-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a specific passage; near one-to-one on memory of the absent beloved as mingled pain and joy.

kurals.tamil:
எனைத்து நினைப்பினும் காயார் அனைத்தன்றோ
காதலர் செய்யும் சிறப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Enaiththu ninaippinum kaayaar anaiththandroa
kaadhalar seyyum sirappu.
kurals.meaning: However much I think of him, he is never angry with me for it; is not that the great kindness my beloved does me?
kurals.elementary: Some people get grumpy if you call them too many times. But the lady in this poem says that no matter how often she thinks about her husband, he never gets cross about it. She feels that is his special gift to her.
kurals.university: The heroine finds consolation in a small, wry point: however much (eṉaittu) she thinks of him, he does not grow angry (kāyār, from kāy, ‘to be angry, to burn’). Aṉaittu aṉṟō, ‘is it not that much?’, makes this the measure of the ciṟappu, the special honour or favour her beloved bestows. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render ciṟappu as ‘great help’ (uṭavi), Solomon Pappaiah as ‘the joy he gives’, and Pope as ‘This honour doth my love on me bestow.’ The humour is gentle: he cannot object to what he cannot see, so her freedom to remember is the one gift his absence still allows. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna says that for one who sees him everywhere and sees everything in him, he is never lost, nor is that person ever lost to him.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita promises that the Lord never withdraws from one who constantly holds him in mind.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved never resents being remembered; Krishna goes further and is never lost to the one who remembers him.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.30 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse; partial fit on a beloved who welcomes constant remembrance, in a theological register.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as patient and slow to anger.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s husband who is never angry, however often he is thought of, embodies love that ‘is not easily provoked’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; partial fit on love’s freedom from anger, without the Kural’s playful point about remembrance.

islam.quote_or_event: In a hadith qudsi God says: I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him when he remembers Me; if he remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself.
islam.explanation: The divine Beloved welcomes and returns every remembrance.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved never resents being remembered; in this hadith the Beloved responds to remembrance with remembrance.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith, wording not checked live; good fit on remembrance welcomed by the beloved, in a theological frame.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hatred stirreth up strifes; but love covereth all transgressions.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts hatred’s quarrels with love’s readiness to pass over offences.
judaism.tie_back: The beloved who never grows angry at being endlessly thought of shows love that covers all things.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); only a general fit on love’s forbearance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Among a husband’s duties to his wife, the Buddha lists honouring her, not disparaging her, being faithful to her, giving her authority in the home and providing her with adornments.
buddhism.explanation: The Sigalovada Sutta sets out a husband’s respectful kindness toward his wife.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband who never grows angry with his wife is a small instance of the non-disparaging regard the Buddha asks of husbands.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutta; only a general fit on a husband’s kindly regard, offered as the next-best match.

jainism.quote_or_event: Samantabhadra tells the Jina that, being free from attachment and having shed all enmity, he has no need of worship and no displeasure at blame, yet remembrance of his virtues purifies the mind of the one who remembers.
jainism.explanation: In Jain devotion the Jina is never angered, however he is thought of, and the benefit of remembering him falls to the devotee.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved is never angry at being remembered; the Jina, beyond all passion, cannot be, though he also feels no affection in return.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of a well-known Digambara hymn, not checked live; structural parallel, with the Jina’s detachment unlike a lover’s indulgence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, married from youth and grown old together in a poor cottage, live in such harmony that when the gods grant them a wish they ask only that neither should outlive the other.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s old couple embody a love without quarrels that lasts a lifetime.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their unruffled mutual devotion is the gentle, never-angry love the Kural’s wife credits to her husband.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known story; only a general fit on conflict-free married love, with no theme of remembrance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says that complaints and reproaches arise mainly in friendships of utility, whereas friends who love one another for their goodness are eager to do each other good and do not quarrel.
philosophy.explanation: Friendship grounded in the other’s goodness is, for Aristotle, free of recrimination.
philosophy.tie_back: The beloved who never grows angry, however much he is thought of, shows the untroubled goodwill of Aristotle’s best friendship.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.13, 1162b (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a specific passage; partial fit on love without complaint, analytic rather than tender.

kurals.tamil:
விளியுமென் இன்னுயிர் வேறல்லம் என்பார்
அளியின்மை ஆற்ற நினைந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Viliyumen innuyir vaerallam enpaar
aliyinmai aatra ninaindhu.
kurals.meaning: My dear life is ebbing away as I keep thinking of the unkindness of him who used to say, ‘We two are not separate.’
kurals.elementary: Imagine a best friend who always said, ‘We are like twins, we will never be apart,’ and then went away. You might feel very sad remembering those words. The lady in this poem feels like that, and the memory makes her heart ache.
kurals.university: The couplet sets the husband’s past words against his present conduct. Vēṟu allam, ‘we are not different’, is his former vow of oneness (Kalaignar: ‘we are one, not two’); aḷiyiṉmai, ‘lack of tender grace’ (aḷi, ‘kindness, compassion’), is how she now reads his absence. Thinking on it too much (āṟṟa niṉaintu), her ‘sweet life’ (iṉṉuyir) is perishing (viḷiyum). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both stress the contrast between what he ‘used to say’ and his present want of love, and Pope renders: ‘Dear life departs, when his ungracious deeds I ponder o’er, / Who said erewhile, “We’re one for evermore.”’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa opens the Raghuvamsha by saluting Parvati and Parameshvara, the parents of the world, as joined together like a word and its meaning.
hinduism.explanation: The image of Shiva and Parvati as inseparable as word and sense is the classical Indian emblem of conjugal oneness.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘We are not separate’ is the ideal the husband once proclaimed; Kalidasa’s divine couple show the oneness the heroine feels has been betrayed.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very famous verse; strong fit on the ideal of conjugal non-separateness, though without the theme of broken promise.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that husband and wife are no longer two but one, and should not be parted.
christianity.tie_back: The husband’s ‘we are not two’ echoes this teaching, which makes his apparent unkindness all the more painful to her.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; strong fit on marital oneness, while the Kural adds the grief of its apparent betrayal.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi tells of a lover who knocked at his beloved’s door and, asked ‘Who is there?’, answered ‘I’, and was turned away; after a year of separation he returned and answered ‘It is you’, and was let in, since there was no room for two I’s in one house.
islam.explanation: The Masnavi presents true love as the end of separateness between lover and beloved.
islam.tie_back: The beloved’s ‘we are not separate’ is Rumi’s ‘It is you’, and the heroine grieves that the oneness seems to have been withdrawn.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book I (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous story; strong fit on lovers ‘not two’, exact verse numbers not checked live.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife, and they shall be one flesh.”
judaism.explanation: Genesis founds marriage on the man cleaving to his wife until the two become one.
judaism.tie_back: The husband’s vow that ‘we are not separate’ is this founding ideal, which his absence now seems to contradict.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); strong fit on marital oneness, without the Kural’s grief.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Canda-Kinnara Jataka, when a king shoots the kinnara Canda to seize his mate, the kinnari Candā laments over her husband, refuses the king, and appeals to the gods until Sakka restores her husband to life.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka celebrates a wife whose devotion holds her husband’s life as inseparable from her own.
buddhism.tie_back: Candā lives the oneness the Kural’s husband once spoke of, and her grief at his loss matches the heroine’s ebbing life.
buddhism.source: Canda-Kinnara Jataka (Jataka 485) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jataka; strong fit on inseparable spouses and lament, though loss is by violence rather than unkindness.

jainism.quote_or_event: On his wedding day Prince Arishtanemi turns back, renounces the world and leaves his bride Rajimati, who, by the tradition of their love through earlier births, had been his companion; she grieves, then follows him into renunciation.
jainism.explanation: The Neminatha-Rajimati story is Jainism’s great tale of a bride left by the one she counted as her own.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati, abandoned by one who had been joined to her, mirrors the heroine wasting at the thought of a beloved who once said ‘we are not separate’, though Jainism praises his departure.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45); the earlier births are told in Hemachandra’s Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 8
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative, not re-checked live; the abandonment parallels the Kural, but Jainism honours the renunciation she mourns.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Alcyone begs her husband Ceyx not to sail, or to take her with him, saying she would rather share any danger than be parted; he goes alone, and she keeps vigil for him, until in the end the gods turn both into kingfishers so that they are never separated again.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s couple, devoted to the point of refusing separation, are finally made inseparable by the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Alcyone grieving a husband who left despite their oneness echoes the heroine wasting away at his apparent lack of tenderness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known story; good fit on grief at separation from a spouse who was ‘one’ with her, though Ceyx is not unkind.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Aristophanes’ speech, Hephaestus offers to weld two lovers into one so that they will be no longer two but one, sharing a single life and a single death, and each lover says this is exactly what he has always longed for.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s Aristophanes defines love as the desire to be made one with the beloved.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘We are not two’ is the lovers’ wish in the Symposium, and the Kural’s heroine suffers because that oneness now seems denied.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 192d-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a specific passage; near one-to-one on the claim of lovers to be ‘not two’.

kurals.tamil:
விடாஅது சென்றாரைக் கண்ணினால் காணப்
படாஅதி வாழி மதி.
kurals.transliteration:
Vitaaadhu sendraaraik kanninaal kaanap
pataaadhi vaazhi madhi.
kurals.meaning: Long may you live, O Moon! Do not set, so that my eyes may find him who has gone away yet never left my heart.
kurals.elementary: When someone you love is far away, you might look up at the moon and think, ‘They can see the moon too!’ The lady in this poem asks the moon not to go down, so that she can keep looking, as if the moon could help her find him.
kurals.university: The heroine addresses the moon (mati) with a blessing (vāḻi, ‘may you live long’) and a plea: paṭāa-ti, ‘do not set’ (paṭu, ‘to go down, set’), so that she may see with her eyes (kaṇṇiṉāl kāṇa) him who left without leaving (viṭāatu ceṉṟār), that is, who went away but never left her heart. Parimelazhagar’s celebrated gloss explains that since the moon is looked at by both lovers, their eyes meet in it, so she ‘sees’ him at least by the measure of the eye. Manakkudavar and Parip Perumal read paṭāatu (‘the moon does not set’) and take it as a complaint: if the moon set, she could sleep and meet him in dreams; Parimelazhagar notes this reading and its sense. Kalingar is reported to have placed this couplet in chapter 127 (avarvayiṉ vitumpal) instead (all as summarised on kuralthiran.com). Pope renders: ‘Set not; so may’st thou prosper, moon! that eyes may see / My love who went away, but ever bides with me.’ The standard text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Meghaduta the exiled Yaksha, separated from his wife, sends a monsoon cloud as his messenger across India, and laments that he can find her likeness only in parts of nature, her face in the moon, her glances in the eyes of startled deer.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s separated lover reaches the beloved through the sky and sees her in the moon.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine pleading with the moon, the Yaksha makes a heavenly body the go-between with his absent spouse.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta, Uttaramegha (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous poem, verse numbers not checked; strong fit on a celestial intermediary and the moon as image of the absent beloved.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon.”
christianity.explanation: Joshua commands the sun and moon to stand still so the day of battle may be completed.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine’s plea ‘do not set’ asks of the moon what Joshua asks, though for love’s sake rather than victory’s.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the shared element is asking the moon to stay, in a very different context.

islam.quote_or_event: Abraham, watching the night sky, sees the moon rise and says ‘This is my lord’, but when it sets he says that unless his Lord guides him he will be among those who go astray, and turns to the One who never sets.
islam.explanation: The Qur’an uses the setting moon to teach that only what never disappears deserves one’s heart.
islam.tie_back: The heroine begs the moon not to set; Abraham learns from its setting to seek a Beloved who never departs, a contrasting use of the same image.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; shares only the image of the setting moon, offered as the best available match.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that whoever blesses the new moon in its proper time is as one who receives the face of the Divine Presence.
judaism.explanation: In the rite of blessing the moon, looking at the moon becomes a way of greeting the unseen Beloved.
judaism.tie_back: Parimelazhagar’s reading, that both lovers’ eyes meet in the moon, has a Jewish counterpart in the moon as a meeting place with an unseen Presence.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; an imaginative structural parallel, not a romantic one.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada names not seeing the beloved as a basic form of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s plea to the moon arises from the very pain the Dhammapada names, though the Buddha’s remedy is to loosen the attachment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; names the same pain but prescribes the opposite response.

jainism.quote_or_event: Encamped by a lake at night, Prince Pavananjaya watches a female cakravaka bird crying in anguish through the night for her mate, and, realising how his neglected wife Anjana must have suffered, he secretly returns to her that same night.
jainism.explanation: The Jain Ramayana uses the night-separated cakravaka birds to awaken a husband to the pain of separation.
jainism.tie_back: The night scene of a pining bird and a husband moved to return matches the Kural’s moonlit night of longing for an absent spouse.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 7, story of Anjana and Pavananjaya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson); also in Vimalasuri’s Paumacariya
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative, not re-checked live; shares the night-time longing but not the address to the moon.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho tells Atthis that their friend, now far away in Lydia, outshines the Lydian women as the rosy-fingered moon after sunset surpasses all the stars, and that she wanders, remembering gentle Atthis with longing.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho uses the moon to link the beloved far away with those who long for her at home.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the moon becomes the shared light that binds separated lovers across distance.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho, fragment 96 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Anne Carson)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested fragment; strong fit on the moon as a link between separated loved ones.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca thanks Lucilius for writing often, saying that if pictures of absent friends are pleasant, a letter is more so, for it brings real traces and real evidence of an absent friend.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca values any token that lets the absent friend be present in some measure.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine seeks such a token in the moon, which both lovers can see and so ‘meet’ in, as Parimelazhagar explains.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 40.1 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a specific letter; parallel on mediated presence of the absent, though about letters and friendship.
